source.title: PEBench: A Fictitious Dataset to Benchmark Machine Unlearning for Multimodal Large Language Models
source.authors: Zhao-Pan Xu; P. Zhou; Wei-Dong Tang; Jia-Xin Ai; Wang-Bo Zhao; Xiao-Jiang Peng; Kai Wang; Yang You; Wen-Qi Shao; Hong-Xun Yao; Kai-Peng Zhang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Parts of Table III are flattened, so its individual method-by-metric values cannot be assigned reliably from this text.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether unlearning methods reduce performance on targeted concepts while assessing retained performance, using a multimodal benchmark and measures different from the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports results for standard unlearning methods and their effects on target efficacy, retained knowledge, and related concepts. It does not apply fine-tuning recovery attacks, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompt-only attacks. Table III contains additional results, but the flattened text does not reliably associate all individual numbers with methods and metrics.
record.test_reason: A multimodal benchmark (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Llama-3.2-Vision-11B) that measures how far five standard methods (GA, GD, KL, PO, DPO) forget fictitious persons and events, and what general ability they keep. This bears on the efficacy-and-utility half of version A in a new setting. It applies no recovery attack, so B–F and A's robustness clause are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also report that Llama-3.2-Vision-11B retains utility better than LLaVA-7B and that performance worsens as the forget set grows. They propose Balanced Gradient Difference (BGD) to ease joint person-and-event unlearning. They draw no conclusion about recovery or about deletion versus blocking.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates several unlearning approaches on synthetic multimodal image-and-event data; it does not reproduce the claim's fine-tuning, activation-ablation, quantization, or prompting recovery procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that efficacy and utility vary by unlearning method and target type, and that performance drifts further from the Goal model as the forget-set proportion increases from 5% to 10% to 15%.

fits_no_version.finding: Unlearning one visual concept degrades a coupled concept in the same image. Event ROUGE-L falls from 88.6 to 46.2 after person unlearning. Person accuracy falls from 96.4% to 55.2% after event unlearning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In multimodal unlearning, forgetting a person or an event damages recognition of the coupled event or person.

record.problems: The paper evaluates synthetic fictional entities and static images. It reports no recovery attacks. The prose gives qualitative efficacy and utility conclusions, while the flattened Table III prevents reliable assignment of many method-specific values from the supplied text. No uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: Table III reports many additional method-, model-, target-, metric-, and forget-proportion-specific results. They were not extracted because the supplied flattened layout does not reliably associate all values with the relevant columns and rows. The study also reports figure-based training-step trends in Figures 7 and 8; no figure-only values were added.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover the forgotten knowledge, and whether it is deleted or only blocked.
All of B: no relearning or fine-tuning attack.
All of C: no activation ablation and no internal analysis.
All of E: no rephrasing, jailbreak, language or in-context attack. The Generality test uses new images of the same targets, not adversarial prompts.
All of F: the proposed BGD method addresses joint person-and-event unlearning, not robustness to attacks.

missing.what: World Fact (POPE) preservation after unlearning, mostly about 78–85 versus baseline 82.3/84.3. This is the general-ability half of A.
Joint person-and-event unlearning: person efficacy drops from an average 99.0 to 86.2, and event efficacy from 47.8 to 45.1.
Per-method, per-model Efficacy and Retain values are readable for several blocks, e.g. LLaVA 5% and Llama 5%.
Larger forget sets (5%→15%) move all methods further from the Goal model.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3: this is a new multimodal setting on fictitious entities, and it measures only surface forgetting. Because there are no attacks, the supports label covers only behavioural forgetting and says nothing about shallowness. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether attacks can recover targeted knowledge after unlearning, or whether the knowledge has been removed from weights rather than made inaccessible.
Recovery by fine-tuning on small, unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples.
Recovery by ablating an activation direction, or analysis establishing blocked access rather than deletion.
Recovery by rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
A newer method's resistance to the recovery attacks in the claim.

rows.subject: PEBench methods (aggregate; models and methods not separated in this statement)
rows.operation_detail: Apply five unlearning methods to person targets and evaluate efficacy.
rows.baseline: Finetuned model is described as the lower bound for unlearning; Goal model as the upper bound.
rows.value: Most methods achieve near-perfect efficacy in person unlearning; most methods achieve high efficacy and generality.
rows.note: The paper gives this qualitative aggregate conclusion but does not state in the prose that the target accuracy reaches near chance.
rows.check: Table III is partly readable. LLaVA 5% person Efficacy: GA, GD and DPO 100.0, KL 99.5, PO 88.4 (Finetune 2.0, Goal 100). Llama 5%: 83.7–100. PO and DPO on Llama are lower, so the effect is near-full rather than uniform.

statements.correction: PEBench (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Llama-3.2-Vision-11B; GA, PO, GD, KL, DPO; no attacks tested). Person Efficacy at 5% forget: LLaVA Finetune 2.0, PO 88.4, GA/GD/DPO 100, KL 99.5; Llama 83.7-100. Person Retain: LLaVA 2.2-35.5 for all methods vs Finetune about 95; Llama 5% GD 82.5 vs 97.7. Event G-Eval efficacy 30.2-59.2 vs Goal 85.3-91.9.
statements.problem: Cites PEBench (R1) but gives none of its results. The numbers listed all belong to other studies; 54.4->3.8 is credited to PPE-Bench and is not in this text. The conditions imply the cited studies tested attacks, but PEBench tested none. It also leaves out PEBench's sharp Retain/Real loss in person unlearning.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Person unlearning, as described qualitatively across the tested methods
reader_labels.reason: The authors report near-perfect efficacy for most methods on person targets (R1).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Person unlearning and retained non-target knowledge
reader_labels.reason: Retention on the Retain and Real sets often degrades, particularly for GA, so strong target forgetting does not consistently preserve utility (R3).
